newsitem.title: CANADA: FIGURE SKATING-STOJKO, SLUTSKAYA WIN SINGLES AT SKATE CANADA.
newsitem.headline: FIGURE SKATING-STOJKO, SLUTSKAYA WIN SINGLES AT SKATE CANADA.

text.p: Former world figure skating champion Elvis Stojko, who failed to medal at the 1996 worlds, returned to the winner's circle Saturday edging Russian Ilia Kulik to win the $30,000 prize at Skate Canada.
Seven judges favoured the Canadian, while the other two gave higher marks to Kulik, who received $18,000 for second place. American Scott Davis earned $10,000 for third.
In the women's singles, Russia's Irina Slutskaya performed a flawless free-skating routine to clinch the title and her $30,000 prize.

The 17-year-old Russian, who won the 1995 world junior title and was seventh at the '95 senior worlds, was hardly pressed as world number two Lu Chen of China withdrew after aggravating a foot injury in practice on Wednesday.
"I wish Lu had skated so we could have competed and fought for places," world number three Slutskaya said through an interpreter.
Second place, and a check for $18,000, went to 14-year-old American Tara Lipinski, with Switzerland's Lucinda Ruh, 17, finishing a surprising third to collect $10,000.

The 24-year-old Stojko, the 1994 and 1995 world champion, landed six triple jumps. He had programmed eight into his routine to music from the movie Dragonheart but he two-footed the landing of one of them and omitted another. He had plotted a quadruple toe-loop attempt, but it was reduced to a triple.
His marks for technical merit were 5.8s and 5.9s, while his artistic marks were from 5.5 to 5.9.

Kulik, 19, who silvered at last March's worlds in Edmonton when Stojko slipped to fourth, also landed six triple jumps. Skating to music from Romeo and Juliet, his mistakes were similar Stojko's -- a double-footed landing and an omission.

While Stojko produced two triple jump-double jump combinations, Kulik executed only one combo, which led to technical marks lower than those awarded Stojko. Kulik's artistic marks were slightly superior to Stojko's, making it a close decision.
